Content

FORMATION OF ROCKS

  • Petrology: The study of rocks is called Petrology.
Age of rocks is calculated using Carbon Dating.

Igneous Rocks

  • Igneous rocks are formed through the cooling and solidification of molten rock, known as magma or lava.

#### Two Types of Igneous Rocks

  1. 1. Intrusive Igneous Rocks / Plutonic Rocks
  • When the magma cools and solidify slowly within the Earth's crust, it forms intrusive igneous rocks. E.g. Granite, Gabbro, etc.
  1. 2. Extrusive Igneous Rocks
  • When the magma erupts on the Earth's surface as lava, it cools and solidifies quickly. This rapid cooling results in the formation of small crystals or glassy texture. E.g. Basalt, Pumice (it floats in water), etc.
Granite is found in Continental crust. Basalt is found in Oceanic crust.

Plutonic Bodies

  • Plutonic bodies, also known as plutons, are large bodies of intrusive igneous rock that form beneath the Earth's surface.

#### Types of Plutonic Bodies

  • Batholiths: A batholith is a large mass of igneous rock that forms deep within the Earth's crust and is exposed at the surface through erosion and uplift.
  • Dykes: Dykes are vertical or steeply inclined sheets of magma that cut across the layers of surrounding rock.
  • Sills: Sills are horizontal sheets of magma that intrude between layers of pre-existing rock.
  • Phacolith: A phacolith is a lens-shaped igneous rock pluton that forms in folded sedimentary rock found at Anticlines and Synclines.
  • Laccoliths: Dome-shaped intrusions with a flat base that push overlying layers upward. It is connected by a pipe-like structure.
  • Lapoliths: These are saucer-shaped intrusions with concave top and bottom.

SEDIMENTARY ROCKS

  • Sedimentary rocks are a type of rock that forms from the accumulation and consolidation of sediments over time.
  • Lithification occurs, it is a process by which loose sediments are transformed into solid sedimentary rock. This occurs through a combination of compaction and cementation over long periods of time.
  • They exist in layers/strata.
  • Fossils are found in sedimentary rocks.

Types of Sedimentary Rocks

  1. 1. Mechanically / Clastically formed: Sandstone, limestone, conglomerate, shale, loess, etc.
  2. 2. Organically formed: Chalk, limestone, coal, geyserite, etc.
  3. 3. Chemically formed: Limestone, halite, chert, etc.

METAMORPHIC ROCK

  • Metamorphic rocks are rocks that form when existing rocks (igneous, sedimentary, or even other metamorphic rocks) are subjected to intense heat, pressure, or volume change, causing them to undergo physical and chemical changes. This process is also called Metamorphism.
  • These rocks are formed by recrystallisation and reorganisation of materials within the original rocks.

Types of Metamorphic Rocks

  1. 1. Thermal Metamorphism
  • Metamorphic rocks formed due to sudden temperature change.
  1. 2. Dynamic Metamorphism
  • Metamorphic rocks formed without any chemical change.
  • These are generally formed as a result of high pressure.

Types of Thermal Metamorphism

  1. 1. Contact Metamorphism
  • It occurs when rocks are altered by intense heat due to their proximity to magma or lava.
  1. 2. Regional Metamorphism
  • It occurs when rocks are subjected to high pressure and temperature.
Quartz is not a rock, it is a mineral.
- Taj Mahal is made of: Metamorphic rock.
- Red Fort is made of: Red sandstone (sedimentary rock).

Metamorphism Transformations

Original RockProcessMetamorphic Rock
Granite (Igneous)MetamorphismGneiss
Shale (Sedimentary)MetamorphismSlate, Schist
Sandstone (Sedimentary)MetamorphismQuartzite
Limestone (Sedimentary)MetamorphismMarble
Basalt/Gabbro (Igneous)MetamorphismAmphibolite
Clay (Sedimentary)MetamorphismSlate

Types of Rock (fact box)

  • Soft rock: Talc
  • Hard rock: Diamond
  • Feldspar consists of 50% of the Earth's crust and is widely used in glass and ceramic industries.
  • Limestone is one of the key minerals used in cement making.
  • Mica is used in electrical industry; constitutes 4% of Earth's crust.

Rock Cycle

  • It is a geological process that describes how the three main types of rock — igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary — change over time.

Acidic vs Basic Rocks

Acidic RocksBasic Rocks
They are high in silica (mostly feldspar and quartz minerals) up to 80%They are poor in silica (mostly feldspar and quartz minerals) about 40%
They are light in colorThey are dark in color
Due to high silica content, acidic magma cools fasterDue to low silica content, basic magma cools slowly
E.g. Granite, Quartz, FeldsparE.g. Basalt, Gabbro, Dolerite

VOLCANO

  • A volcano is a geological feature formed by the eruption of molten rock (magma) from beneath the Earth's crust.

Types of Volcano

  1. 1. Cinder cone: They are small, steep-sided volcanoes formed by moderately explosive eruptions.
  2. 2. Flood Basalt Province: These volcanoes outpour, highly fluid lava that flows for long distances. E.g. Deccan Traps (in West Central region).
  3. 3. Shield: They are primarily formed by eruption of basaltic lava which is non-viscous fluid. E.g. Kilauea Volcano in Hawaii, USA.
  4. 4. Composite: They are generally cooler and viscous in nature. E.g. Mt. Chimborazo and Mt. Fuzi (also known as Stratovolcano).
  5. 5. Caldera: It is the most explosive types of volcano, it collapses on itself.

Geyser

  • A geyser is a hot spring that intermittently erupts steam and hot water due to geothermal activity beneath the Earth's surface.
  • Geysers are commonly found in areas of volcanic activity because the heat from magma or hot rocks below the Earth's surface heats the groundwater, leading to the formation of geysers.
- Highest volcano: Ojas del Salado (it is located between Chile and Argentina in Andes mountain range).
- Lighthouse of Mediterranean: Mount Stromboli

CONTINENTS AND OCEAN

  • In 1912, Alfred Wegener gave Continental Drift Theory.
  • All of the modern day continents had previously been clunk together in a supercontinent called Pangaea and the water body is called Panthalassa.

Evidences

  • Jig-saw fit.
  • Fossil deposits (Palaentology is the study of Fossils).
  • Placer deposits (gold).
  • Botanical evidences.
  • Rocks of same age across the oceans.

Reason for Continental Drift

  1. 1. Tidal force
  2. 2. Polar fleeing force
As suggested by Alfred Wegener
  • Actual reason was later given by Arthur Holmes in 1930.
  • Continental drift occurs due to the movement of tectonic plates, which is driven by convection cells in the Earth's mantle.
  • The heat that drives convection cells in the Earth's mantle and plate motion comes mainly from three sources:
  1. 1. Radioactive decay of elements.
  2. 2. Residual heat from the Earth's formation about 4.6 billion years ago when gravitational energy was converted into heat.
  3. 3. Latent heat released by the solidification of the Earth's core as it cools down.

FACTS

  • Mariana Trench is the deepest part of the Pacific Ocean (11 km).
  • Challenger Deep is the deepest known point in Mariana Trench.
  • Atlantic Ocean is the busiest ocean. Sargasso Sea is a unique region in the Atlantic Ocean, which is a borderless sea (brown algae Sargassum is seen here).

Milankovitch Theory

  • It describes the collective effects of changes in Earth's movement on its climate over thousands of years.
  • In 1596, Abraham Ortelius's work, "Thesaurus Geographicus", first suggested that Earth's continents were not always in their current locations.

SEAFLOOR SPREADING

  • Harry H. Hess in 1962, gave Seafloor Spreading Theory.
  • Seafloor Spreading is a process by which new oceanic crust is formed at mid-ocean, due to divergent plate boundary. The magma erupts from beneath pushing the older crossed away from the ridge in the centre.
  • The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is a mid-ocean ridge located along the floor of the Atlantic Ocean, and part of the longest relief feature in the world.
  • It got created due to divergent plate boundary.

Relief Features

Relief features are of two types:

  1. 1. Major Relief Features
  • Four major relief features are there: Continental Shelf → Continental Slope → Continental Rise → Abyssal plain / Deep sea plains
  1. 2. Minor Relief Features
  • E.g. Seamount, Guyot (flat-topped sea mount), Mid-Ocean ridge, Trench, Coral, Atoll, etc.
- Continental Shelf is the shallowest part of the ocean, having a gradient of 1° or less.
- The gradient of the Continental Slope region varies between 2–5°.

Corals

  • Corals are marine organisms known as "Rainforest of Sea".
  • They exist in symbiotic relationship with Zooxanthella algae. The corals secrete CaCO₃ that provides protection to the algae and in return the algae make food for the corals.
  • The corals exists in colony.

Favourable Conditions Required for Corals to Survive

  1. 1. Saline water (they cannot survive in fresh water).
  2. 2. Sunlight.
  3. 3. Clear water.
  4. 4. Temperature (they require moderate temperature: 30°–35°C).
Great Barrier Reef in Australia is the largest barrier reef (colony of corals) in the world.

Coral Bleaching

  • When water is too warm, corals will expel the algae (Zooxanthella) living in their tissues, causing the coral to turn completely white. Climate change is a major key factor in this change.

FACTS

  • Petroleum is extracted from Continental Shelf (start of ocean basin and is very narrow).
  • Siberian Shelf in the Arctic Ocean is the widest Continental Shelf (1500 km wide).
  • West Coast of South America is the narrowest Continental Shelf.

Key concepts

  • Petrology is the study of rocks. Rock age is calculated by Carbon Dating.
  • Igneous rocks — formed by cooling/solidification of magma/lava. Intrusive/Plutonic (slow cooling inside crust, e.g. Granite, Gabbro); Extrusive (rapid cooling on surface, small crystals/glassy, e.g. Basalt, Pumice — Pumice floats on water).
  • Granite = Continental crust; Basalt = Oceanic crust.
  • Plutonic bodies (plutons) = large intrusive igneous rock bodies beneath surface. Types: Batholiths (deep, exposed by erosion/uplift), Dykes (vertical/steeply inclined sheets cutting across layers), Sills (horizontal sheets between layers), Phacolith (lens-shaped, at Anticlines/Synclines), Laccoliths (dome-shaped, flat base, connected by pipe), Lapoliths (saucer-shaped).
  • Sedimentary rocks — accumulation and consolidation of sediments via lithification (compaction + cementation); exist in layers; contain fossils. Types: Mechanically/clastically (Sandstone, limestone, conglomerate, shale, loess), Organically (Chalk, limestone, coal, geyserite), Chemically (Limestone, halite, chert).
  • Metamorphic rocks — existing rocks altered by intense heat/pressure/volume change (metamorphism); recrystallisation and reorganisation. Thermal (sudden temperature change) → Contact (heat from nearby magma/lava) / Regional (high pressure + temperature). Dynamic (high pressure, no chemical change).
  • Metamorphic transformations: Granite → Gneiss; Shale → Slate, Schist; Sandstone → Quartzite; Limestone → Marble; Basalt/Gabbro → Amphibolite; Clay → Slate.
  • Rock facts: Talc = softest; Diamond = hardest; Feldspar = 50% of crust (used in glass/ceramics); Limestone = used in cement; Mica = electrical industry, 4% of crust.
  • Quartz is a mineral, not a rock. Taj Mahal = metamorphic rock. Red Fort = red sandstone (sedimentary).
  • Rock cycle: Igneous ⇄ Sedimentary ⇄ Metamorphic via melting/cooling, heat/pressure, uplift/erosion.
  • Acidic rocks (high silica ≤80%, light colour, cool fast, e.g. Granite, Quartz, Feldspar) vs Basic rocks (low silica ~40%, dark colour, cool slowly, e.g. Basalt, Gabbro, Dolerite).
  • Volcano — eruption of molten magma. Types: Cinder cone (small, steep, moderately explosive), Flood Basalt Province (fluid lava, long flows, e.g. Deccan Traps in West Central), Shield (basaltic, non-viscous fluid, e.g. Kilauea, Hawaii), Composite (cool, viscous, e.g. Mt. Chimborazo, Mt. Fuzi/Stratovolcano), Caldera (most explosive, collapses on itself).
  • Highest volcano: Ojas del Salado (Chile–Argentina border, Andes). Lighthouse of Mediterranean: Mount Stromboli.
  • Geyser — hot spring that intermittently erupts steam and hot water from geothermal activity.
  • Continental Drift Theory (Alfred Wegener, 1912): all continents were once one supercontinent Pangaea surrounded by Panthalassa ocean; Tethys Sea inside.
  • Evidences of continental drift: jig-saw fit, fossil deposits (Palaeontology), placer deposits (gold), botanical evidences, same-age rocks across oceans.
  • Reasons for continental drift (Wegener): Tidal force + Polar fleeing force. Actual reason (Arthur Holmes, 1930): convection cells in the mantle driven by (1) radioactive decay of elements, (2) residual heat from Earth's formation 4.6 billion years ago (gravitational energy → heat), (3) latent heat from solidification of the core.
  • Mariana Trench = deepest part of Pacific (11 km); Challenger Deep = deepest point in Mariana Trench. Atlantic Ocean = busiest ocean. Sargasso Sea = unique borderless sea in Atlantic (brown algae Sargassum).
  • Milankovitch Theory — collective effects of Earth's movement changes on climate over thousands of years. Abraham Ortelius (1596, Thesaurus Geographicus) first suggested continents were not always in current locations.
  • Seafloor Spreading (Harry H. Hess, 1962): new oceanic crust forms at mid-ocean ridges via divergent plate boundary; older crust pushed away. Mid-Atlantic Ridge = part of the longest relief feature in the world; created by divergent plate boundary. Oceanic crust is younger than continental crust; age of oceanic rocks increases away from mid-ocean ridge.
  • Relief features:
  • Major (4): Continental Shelf → Continental Slope → Continental Rise → Abyssal plain / Deep sea plains. Continental Shelf = shallowest (gradient ≤1°); Continental Slope gradient = 2–5°.
  • Minor: Seamount, Guyot (flat-topped seamount), Mid-Ocean ridge, Trench, Coral, Atoll, Submarine canyon, Abyssal hill, etc.
  • Petroleum is extracted from the Continental Shelf (start of ocean basin, narrow). Siberian Shelf (Arctic) = widest (1500 km). West Coast of South America = narrowest.
  • Corals = "Rainforest of Sea"; symbiotic with Zooxanthella algae; secrete CaCO₃; exist in colony. Favourable: saline water, sunlight, clear water, 30–35°C. Great Barrier Reef (Australia) = largest barrier reef in the world.
  • Coral bleaching — when water is too warm, corals expel Zooxanthella algae, turning white. Climate change is a major factor.
